precepts.text: Now there were in the church that was at Antioch certain prophets and teachers; as Barnabas, and Simeon that was called Niger, and Lucius of Cyrene. They were called what? Niger means black. The white man uses that term as a derogatory word, but the prophets were called black right through history. So if the prophets were black, that means Christ was too. And the same way we are called that today, nothing has changed.
precepts.point: That is the antichrist system right there. This whole religious system that you see set up is part of the antichrist system, because Christianity is against the true Christ. Judaism is against the true Christ. If you tell them that Jesus Christ is black, do you think they want to hear that? They do not want to hear that. We are the true anointed. But the world calls us a hate group. They say we are hateful for the teachings of Christ. They say you all are black extremists, because we say that we are the Jews and we are the believers of Christ.

note.label: Lucifer: The Antichrist

precepts.why:
Christ said many would come in his name and deceive many by changing who he and his people are. So look at what the apostles and prophets were called: “Now there were in the church that was at Antioch certain prophets and teachers; as Barnabas, and Simeon that was called Niger, and Lucius of Cyrene.”

They were called what? Niger means black. The white man uses that term as a derogatory word, but the prophets were called black right through history. So if the prophets were black, what does that mean Christ was? Black too.

And the same way they were called that then, we are called that today. Nothing has changed. The people of the Bible were black, which is why the false Christ of Christianity, the white Jesus, is a deception. Christianity is built on white supremacy, on murder and bloodshed, and those who come in Christ's name with a white image are against the Christ of the Bible.

precepts.text: And to this agree the words of the prophets; as it is written. As it is written. Meaning they had to go back and search. Wait, this was written here. So it makes sense what happened in this particular place of the book, because the prophets wrote about it. That is precept upon precept. Not Hebrew hopscotch. That is understanding the history.
precepts.point: As it is also written. As it is written.

note.label: Give Diligence

precepts.why:
Paul declares that God “hath raised up Jesus again; as it is also written in the second psalm, Thou art my Son, this day have I begotten thee.” As it is also written. Acts 15 says the same thing when the apostles came together: “And to this agree the words of the prophets; as it is written”.

As it is written means they had to go back and search: wait, this was written here. What happened in that particular place of the book makes sense because the prophets wrote about it. The glad tidings Paul preached were not something new; they were the promise made unto the fathers, fulfilled unto their children, and the prophets had already written it.

That is precept upon precept. Christians call it Hebrew hopscotch and cherry-picking, but it is studying and understanding the word of God, understanding the history and what things must take place. The apostles themselves did it: they took what was happening and laid it beside what the prophets wrote.

Those who do not have the spirit of the Lord cannot do it, and they want to shame us for having understanding and being able to go from Genesis to Revelation and give the understanding thereof. We are going to keep on going precept upon precept, confounding you negroes, because that is how the apostles taught: as it is written.

precepts.text: There were in the church that was at Antioch certain prophets and teachers; as Barnabas, and Simeon that was called Niger. It was never derogatory.
precepts.point: The word of the Lord that came to Micah the Morasthite: the word Moor, Morasthite, is in the Bible. Micah, teacher of the Moors.

note.label: We Are Born in Babylon

precepts.why:
“Now there were in the church that was at Antioch certain prophets and teachers; as Barnabas, and Simeon that was called Niger”. Right there among the prophets and teachers of the church is a man called Niger. It was never derogatory. It was a name for our people, used in the church itself, set alongside Barnabas, Lucius of Cyrene, Manaen and Saul.

That is the same thing as Micah the Morasthite in Micah 1:1. The word Moor is in the Bible: Micah, teacher of the Moors. These names were ours, and they described our people plainly. The names that came later were put on us by others: the Latins, who later became the Romans, gave the name Africa to the region around Carthage and Utica. Africa was a term that came way later.

So we have to go back to the name God calls us. Simeon called Niger and Micah the Morasthite were Israelites, teachers and prophets of our people, and the scriptures show them to us by those names without any shame in them.

precepts.text: The God of this people of Israel chose our fathers, and exalted the people when they dwelt as strangers in the land of Egypt. So those strangers are the nation of Israel.
precepts.point: But now in Christ Jesus ye who sometimes were far off are made nigh by the blood of Christ. Who was afar off? Israel. These Ephesians in Ephesus are Israelites scattered in Ephesus. He is our peace: not everybody's peace. Christ is the peace that brings both nations, the southern and northern kingdom, back together.

note.label: The Colossians & The CHRISTIANS of America

precepts.why:
Ephesians 2:12 says that at that time they were “without Christ, being aliens from the commonwealth of Israel, and strangers from the covenants of promise, having no hope, and without God in the world.” Christians will say, well, you have to deal with those strangers. So let's see who the strangers are.

“The God of this people of Israel chose our fathers, and exalted the people when they dwelt as strangers in the land of Egypt.” The book of Acts is saying that the God of Israel chose our fathers, so the people Paul was speaking to in Antioch were Israelites. And who dwelt as strangers in the land of Egypt? The nation of Israel.

So those strangers are the Israelites. The scripture calls Israel strangers, and that is who Ephesians is speaking to when it says strangers from the covenants of promise.

So the same thing Paul and Barnabas encountered, with the Jews rejecting salvation in Jesus Christ, is the same thing Christ had to deal with.

note.label: Raising Up the Tabernacle of David That Fell

precepts.why:
“But when the Jews saw the multitudes, they were filled with envy, and spake against those things which were spoken by Paul, contradicting and blaspheming.” The same thing that happened with Paul happened with Christ: “After these things Jesus walked in Galilee: for he would not walk in Jewry, because the Jews sought to kill him.”

Christ was not walking with the southern kingdom any more. He went to Galilee, and Matthew 4:15 shows you who was in Galilee: Zebulun and Naphtali, “Galilee of the Gentiles”. Those Gentiles are the northern kingdom.

So the same thing Paul and Barnabas met, the Jews rejecting salvation in Jesus Christ, is the same thing Christ had to deal with. And Paul did what Christ did: “seeing ye put it from you, and judge yourselves unworthy of everlasting life, lo, we turn to the Gentiles.”

The word had to be spoken to Judah “first”, as the Lord “shall save the tents of Judah first”. When Judah put it from them, Christ went into Galilee, and Paul and Barnabas turned to the Gentiles: the northern kingdom. You cannot just assume that because it says Gentiles it means the other nations; there are times it refers to the Israelites in a Gentile state, cut off from being his people in Hosea chapter 1.

And the house of Joseph is Ephraim and the rest: that's the Samaritans and Gentiles in Matthew 10:5. So Christ says the exact same thing: don't go to the Samaritans or Gentiles, the house of Joseph, but rather to the lost sheep, the house of Jacob, the southern kingdom.

note.label: Raising Up the Tabernacle of David That Fell

precepts.why:
Obadiah shows Samaritans, Gentiles and Israel at the same time: “And the house of Jacob shall be a fire, and the house of Joseph a flame, and the house of Esau for stubble”.

The house of Jacob in verse 18 is Judah alone: the southern kingdom, Judah, Benjamin and Levi. The house of Joseph is Ephraim and the rest, the northern kingdom. That is who the Samaritans and Gentiles are in Matthew 10:5.

So when Christ tells his disciples not to go to the Samaritans or the Gentiles, the house of Joseph, but rather to the lost sheep, the house of Jacob, he is saying the exact same thing Paul says here: “It was necessary that the word of God should first have been spoken to you”. First to Judah, the southern kingdom; then “lo, we turn to the Gentiles”, the house of Joseph.

And both houses are brought together against Esau: “they shall kindle in them, and devour them; and there shall not be any remaining of the house of Esau; for the Lord hath spoken it.” Judah received the gospel first, and then the Lord showed the other tribes, and that order has always been the same.

precepts.text: Through this man is preached unto you the forgiveness of sins: and by him all that believe are justified from all things, from which ye could not be justified by the law of Moses. There were sins that had no sacrifice under Moses, like witchcraft: the penalty was death. But under Christ, all that believe are justified from all things.
precepts.point: Blotting out the handwriting of ordinances that was against us, which was contrary to us, and took it out of the way, nailing it to his cross. The subject has not changed: they were beguiling Israel to go back to animal sacrifice, and they did not understand that animal sacrifice was a symbol of what Christ would do for us.

note.label: Deceived by Enticing Words: Colossians 2

precepts.why:
“Be it known unto you therefore, men and brethren, that through this man is preached unto you the forgiveness of sins.” You get forgiveness of sins through this man, Christ. “And by him all that believe are justified from all things”: justified, forgiven, from all things.

Like what? Witchcraft, homosexuality. Using drugs falls under witchcraft: I smoke weed, it open my mind, I see yonder soul. That's a demon. There was no ox or lamb for witchcraft; under Moses you died. Suffer not a witch to live: kill them. But under Christ, all that believe are justified from all things, “from which ye could not be justified by the law of Moses.”

The blood of bulls, goats, oxen and sheep could not give forgiveness for certain sins. That is what “having forgiven you all trespasses” means in Colossians 2:13: when we come into this truth, everything we have done is forgiven. A new slate.

note.label: Called to Judge: Commanded to Be Just

precepts.why:
“Separate me Barnabas and Saul for the work whereunto I have called them.” When the Bishop says separate that brother for the work, he is not talking about Atlanta. He is not talking about Miami or California. Did Israel only scatter in Atlanta? Did Israel only scatter in America? Separate them for the work means no matter where the work is, you have to go there.

The prophecy shows where the work is: “And the Lord shall scatter you among the nations”. Not in America, not in Florida: among the nations. “and ye shall be left few in number among the heathen, whither the Lord shall lead you.” You know what that scripture is saying? No matter where you go, you are going to see Israelites. That is why a judge must be able to travel. Captain Joham just came from Trinidad and Suriname keeping Passover with the brothers there.

So the work Barnabas and Saul were separated for is the same work now: going to the nations where the Lord scattered Israel. It was the Most High God who called you, not the bishop, deacon or captain, and once hands are laid on you, you are sent away. When the phone call comes to travel, we do not want to hear anything from you but yes. Paul travelled, departing unto Seleucia and sailing to Cyprus, and we continue the Acts of the Apostles, bringing the good news all over the world, whatever hate we get for it.

precepts.text: The land of Zabulon, and the land of Nephthalim, by the way of the sea, beyond Jordan, Galilee of the Gentiles. The scripture calls the northern kingdom Gentiles.
precepts.point: Paul and Barnabas waxed bold: it was necessary that the word of God should first have been spoken to you, Judah; but seeing ye put it from you, lo, we turn to the Gentiles. Who are these Gentiles?

note.label: Recovering the Remnant: Worldwide Blitz

precepts.why:
Paul and Barnabas tell Judah, “It was necessary that the word of God should first have been spoken to you”, but the scribes and them were rejecting it, so “lo, we turn to the Gentiles.” Before that, those scattered abroad after the persecution about Stephen were “preaching the word to none but unto the Jews only”: only to the tribe of Judah. So who are the Gentiles they turned to?

Matthew answers it: “The land of Zabulon, and the land of Nephthalim, by the way of the sea, beyond Jordan, Galilee of the Gentiles.” Zabulon and Nephthalim are tribes of the northern kingdom, and the scripture calls them Gentiles. When Paul and Barnabas turned to the Gentiles, they turned to the northern kingdom Israelites.

That is what the vision of Peter in Acts 10 was about. Peter said “it is an unlawful thing for a man that is a Jew to keep company, or come unto one of another nation”. Christians use that to say other races, but Ezekiel shows the two kingdoms were two nations: “they shall be no more two nations, neither shall they be divided into two kingdoms any more at all.” Judah was a nation and the kingdom of Israel, Ephraim and the rest, was a nation. And Peter’s own words about Cornelius and his kin folk are “The word which God sent unto the children of Israel, preaching peace by Jesus Christ”.

Acts 15 looks back on Acts 10: “After this I will return, and will build again the tabernacle of David, which is fallen down”. The kingdom was split, Judah, Benjamin and Levi on one side, Ephraim and the rest on the other. Turning to the Gentiles is God bringing the northern kingdom and the southern kingdom back together, the regathering of the twelve tribes.

precepts.text: Through this man is preached the forgiveness of sins, and by him all that believe are justified from all things from which ye could not be justified by the law of Moses: all things, not almost all.
precepts.point: The veil on Moses' face symbolised Christ and Israel's blindness to the end of that which is abolished; the same veil is on the Pharisees in the reading of the Old Testament, blinded by their covetousness so they had him killed, and it is done away in Christ when they turn to the Lord. Where the Spirit of the Lord is, there is liberty: atonement for all the things you could not atone under Moses.

note.label: Navigating Through Paul's Letters: Works Of The Law & Liberty

precepts.why:
Paul says we are “able ministers of the new testament; not of the letter, but of the spirit: for the letter killeth, but the spirit giveth life.” The letter is the old testament, the Mosaic law of sacrifice. The spirit is Christ's death. The letter kills: if you despised Moses' law, you died without mercy. We read earlier that almost all things are purged with blood. Almost all things you could atone for, if there was an animal for it. But if there was no animal for it, whose blood got shed? Yours. That is condemnation, and condemnation and death are the same.

How does the spirit give life? “Be it known unto you therefore, men and brethren, that through this man is preached unto you the forgiveness of sins”. That is life. “And by him all that believe are justified from all things”. Not almost all things: all things. Everything you can think of, Christ died for, which the animals could not do. You can repent under Christ's death; under animals, you cannot.

“from which ye could not be justified by the law of Moses”: that law is the sacrifice, the law of sin and death, the ministration of condemnation. That is why Paul said in Galatians that if you want to go by that sacrifice, you are a debtor to do the whole law, including sacrificing animals, and the temple is destroyed, so you had better figure it out.

So the ministration of death, “written and engraven in stones”, was glorious, but “much more doth the ministration of righteousness exceed in glory”, because under Christ you can atone for everything you could not atone for under Moses. “where the Spirit of the Lord is, there is liberty”: freedom from the law of sin and death.

precepts.text: Through this man is preached unto you the forgiveness of sins, and by him all that believe are justified from all things, from which ye could not be justified by the law of Moses. Animals could not atone for all things; Christ's death does. That is the difference.
precepts.point: Cursed is every one that hangeth on a tree. The lynchings of our people from trees, lamps, and bridges were not coincidental. Christ nailed to a wooden cross hung by his hands and feet for hours: that is a lynching, and Christ died a black man's death. That the blessing of Abraham might come on the Gentiles through Jesus Christ, that we might receive the promise of the Spirit through faith.

note.label: Navigating Through Paul's Letters: Walking Through Galatians

precepts.why:
“But that no man is justified by the law in the sight of God, it is evident: for, The just shall live by faith.” Justified by the law here is the same law as the works of the law in verses 2, 5 and 10 and in Galatians 2:16: the law of sacrifice.

Paul preached the same thing in Acts 13: “Be it known unto you therefore, men and brethren, that through this man is preached unto you the forgiveness of sins: And by him all that believe are justified from all things, from which ye could not be justified by the law of Moses.” Through Christ is preached the forgiveness of sins, and all that believe in Christ's death are justified from all things, all sins.

Could you receive justification from all things under Moses? No, because animals do not atone for all things. Does Christ's death atone for all things, reconcile us from all things, justify us from all things? Yes. That is the difference.

And the law is not of faith because faith came first. “The man that doeth them shall live in them”: the man who does the sacrifices lives until he commits a sin worthy of death, and then he cannot live anymore. The just live by faith in the one whose death covers what no animal could.

precepts.text: When the Jews saw the multitudes they were filled with envy. Paul said it was necessary the word should first be spoken to you, but seeing ye put it from you, lo, we turn to the Gentiles. Paul went to the northern kingdom, not the Arabs or the Chinese.
precepts.point: If the casting away of them be the reconciling of the world: reconcile means bringing back together what was together before, and the nations were never together with us. Isaiah 45:17 calls Israel the world without end, and Mark 10:30 speaks of the world to come. The receiving of them will be life from the dead, as Ephesians 2:1 says of those dead in trespasses and sins.

note.label: The Dividing Hatred: the Grafted in Strangers

precepts.why:
Here is Romans 11:11 happening in history. “But when the Jews saw the multitudes, they were filled with envy”: that is Judah, filled with jealousy. They “spake against those things which were spoken by Paul, contradicting and blaspheming.”

“Then Paul and Barnabas waxed bold, and said, It was necessary that the word of God should first have been spoken to you”: to the southern kingdom, first. “but seeing ye put it from you, and judge yourselves unworthy of everlasting life, lo, we turn to the Gentiles.” They rejected it, so Paul turned to the Gentiles, who are not a people: the northern kingdom.

You won't find it in the Bible that Israel rejected the prophets and the prophets went to the Arabs. Isaiah never said, they reject me, I'm going to go talk to the Philistines. Lo, we turn to the East Indians, lo, we turn to the Chinese? Christ is black and you're not, there are twelve gates and your name's not on them, but serve him anyway? That makes no sense. Whether you are a black Hebrew Israelite or a Christian, if you teach that, you hate your people. He showeth his word unto Jacob and has not dealt so with any other nation, and still you look for some way to save the people who destroyed, raped, robbed and murdered your people, and don't want judgment to come to them.

So the Gentiles Paul turned to were his own flesh, the northern kingdom, “for to provoke them to jealousy”, that he might “provoke to emulation them which are my flesh, and might save some of them.”

precepts.text: I delight to do thy will, O my God: yea, thy law is within my heart. So what is the will of God? The laws of God. So what is it that pleased God in David, to the point that he established David as ruler over not only his sovereign country but his people as a sovereign government? He pleased the Lord in keeping God's commandments. He kept the commandments. He kept the testimonies.
precepts.point: Which shall fulfil all my will. Which shall fulfil all the Lord's will. Not your own personal will, not your own personal desire. The Lord establishes his rulers by who is faithful to him. Who is faithful to the commandments.

note.label: Sovereign Idiocracy

precepts.why:
Why is it that the Lord established David over his people, to establish the sovereign kingdom of Israel? If you want to be sovereign, there is one way to it: a one-way road with one victory at the end of it, the kingdom of heaven.

“And afterward they desired a king: and God gave unto them Saul the son of Cis.” Even though we wanted a king, it was still the Lord that had to establish him. “And when he had removed him”: the Lord removed Saul from being king over Israel. So where does this power and authority come from? Only from God. Only God can make you sovereign and remove your sovereignty; not you, and not your piece of paper with weird words on it. “he raised up unto them David to be their king”: as righteous and powerful and mighty as David was, it was still the Lord that established him as king over Israel, a sovereign government.

“I have found David the son of Jesse, a man after mine own heart, which shall fulfil all my will.” That is the caveat to being sovereign, to ruling over God's heritage: a man after God's own heart, exactly how the Lord wanted his servant and king to be. And he fulfils all the Lord's will, not his own personal will or desire.

What is the will of God? David says it: “I delight to do thy will, O my God: yea, thy law is within my heart.” The will of God is the laws of God. What pleased God in David, to the point that he established him as ruler over his people as a sovereign government? He kept God's commandments; he kept the testimonies. The Lord establishes his rulers by who is faithful to him, faithful to the commandments.

precepts.text: When he had removed Saul, he raised up unto them David to be their king: I have found David the son of Jesse, a man after mine own heart, which shall fulfil all my will.
precepts.point: The Lord hath sought him a man after his own heart to be captain over his people. Samuel prophesied this without ever having met the replacement; that man is David, predestined before he is even introduced in the scriptures.

note.label: 1 Samuel 13: Make Not Haste in Time of Trouble

precepts.why:
Samuel told Saul, “the Lord hath sought him a man after his own heart, and the Lord hath commanded him to be captain over his people”. Samuel prophesied this without ever having met the replacement.

Paul names him: “And when he had removed him, he raised up unto them David to be their king; to whom also he gave testimony, and said, I have found David the son of Jesse, a man after mine own heart, which shall fulfil all my will.” That man is David, predestined before he is even introduced in the scriptures. Saul had not kept that which the Lord commanded; David was the one which shall fulfil all his will.

precepts.text: Through Christ is preached forgiveness, justifying believers from things the law of Moses could not.
precepts.point: As far as the east is from the west, so far He removes our transgressions; He pities them that fear Him, for He knows we are dust.

note.label: Psalm 103: Bless the Lord for His Benefits to Israel

precepts.why:
“He hath not dealt with us after our sins; nor rewarded us according to our iniquities.” Paul preached what that mercy is: “Be it known unto you therefore, men and brethren, that through this man is preached unto you the forgiveness of sins: And by him all that believe are justified from all things, from which ye could not be justified by the law of Moses.”

Through Christ is preached the forgiveness of sins, justifying believers from things the law of Moses could not justify them from. Christ came to forgive Israel of their sins; that is the not dealing with us after our sins.

That mercy and grace is to Israel, and it is not so that we could continue in sin. As far as the east is from the west, so far he removes our transgressions, and he pities them that fear him.

precepts.text: Through Christ the forgiveness of sins is preached, and all who believe are justified from things the law of Moses could not justify, since some sins in that law required our blood.
precepts.point: His compassion and mercy is another word for grace. He is good to all, and His tender mercies are over all His works.

note.label: Psalm 145: The Greatness and Mercy of the Most High

precepts.why:
“The Lord is gracious, and full of compassion; slow to anger, and of great mercy.” His compassion and mercy is another word for grace. “Be it known unto you therefore, men and brethren, that through this man is preached unto you the forgiveness of sins: And by him all that believe are justified from all things, from which ye could not be justified by the law of Moses.”

Through Christ the forgiveness of sins is preached, and all who believe are justified from things the law of Moses could not justify, since some sins in that law required our blood. That is the great goodness they shall abundantly utter the memory of.

precepts.text: The word of this salvation is sent to the children of the stock of Abraham, the lineage passing through Isaac and Jacob to the twelve tribes.
precepts.point: Paul quotes Hosea and Isaiah, not Jeremiah or Ezekiel, because his subject is the northern kingdom broken before the Assyrian captivity, and his "whosoever" is whosoever of Zion, whosoever of Israel. The Most High called a people not of the Jews only but also of the "Gentiles," meaning Ephraim.

note.label: Acts 10: Cornelius and the Northern Kingdom Grafted In

precepts.why:
“Men and brethren, children of the stock of Abraham, and whosoever among you feareth God, to you is the word of this salvation sent.”

The word of this salvation is sent to the children of the stock of Abraham, the lineage passing through Isaac and Jacob to the twelve tribes. The whosoever that feareth God is among them, just as Cornelius was “one that feareth God.”

precepts.point: Habakkuk 2:4 says the just shall live by his faith, meaning the justified seed of Israel shall live by faith in Christ rather than by animal sacrifice.

note.label: Galatians 2: The Council at Jerusalem and Justification by Faith

precepts.why:
Acts clarifies which law Paul means: “Be it known unto you therefore, men and brethren, that through this man is preached unto you the forgiveness of sins: And by him all that believe are justified from all things, from which ye could not be justified by the law of Moses.”

Under the law of Moses, animal sacrifice, you could not be justified for certain sins like homosexuality, adultery, witchcraft: you were put to death. Through Christ is preached forgiveness of sins, and all that believe are justified from all things. That is the faith of Jesus Christ by which we are justified, and not by the works of that law.
